result: The manuscript provides background on clustered protocadherins (cPcdhs) and Dscam1 systems in neuronal self-avoidance, describing their gene organization, expression patterns, and the challenge of generating neuronal diversity with fewer than 60 cPcdh isoforms compared to ~19,000 Dscam1 isoforms.
evaluation: Claims C1-C22 are well-supported by citations to prior literature and established knowledge. These claims provide essential background context for the study and accurately represent the current understanding of cPcdh biology, gene organization, and expression patterns in different neuronal cell types.

result: Prior structural and biophysical studies have established that cPcdhs interact in trans through antiparallel EC1-4 interactions and in cis through asymmetric EC5-6 interactions, with cPcdhs presented on cell surfaces as cis dimers.
evaluation: Claims C23-C27 accurately summarize prior structural and biophysical work on cPcdh interactions, supported by multiple citations to published crystal structures and functional studies. This provides the structural foundation for interpreting the current study's findings.

result: The 'isoform-mismatch chain-termination model' proposes that cPcdhs form extended zipper-like lattices through alternating cis and trans interactions, with chain growth terminated by isoform mismatches, providing a mechanism for neuronal self-recognition.
evaluation: Claims C28-C32 accurately describe the chain-termination model from prior work, supported by citations to Rubinstein et al., 2015, Brasch et al., 2019, and related studies. The model provides the theoretical framework that motivates the current experimental investigation of cPcdh binding specificity.

result: The study finds that cPcdh trans homophilic interactions are remarkably precise with no heterophilic interactions detected, while cis interactions are largely promiscuous but with relatively weak intrasubfamily and homophilic interactions.
evaluation: Claims C33-C34 represent the main conclusions of the study, supported by comprehensive SPR and AUC experimental data presented in Figures 2 and 4. The binary specificity of trans interactions and the promiscuous but preferential nature of cis interactions are clearly demonstrated by the experimental results.

result: SPR experiments with biotinylated EC1-4 fragments from six representative cPcdh isoforms revealed strictly homophilic trans binding with no heterophilic interactions detected, even between highly similar isoforms (β6/8 with 92% identity and γA8/9 with 82% identity).
evaluation: Claims C35-C41 are well-supported by SPR data in Figure 2A and AUC validation in Figure 2-source data 1. The experimental design is sound, with appropriate controls including trans interface mutants (C41) that confirm binding occurs via the expected interface. The estimated lower limit KD of ~200 μM for heterophilic interactions (C40) is a reasonable inference from detection limits.

result: C-type cPcdhs also exhibit strictly homophilic trans binding, with each of four C-type fragments (αC2, γC3, γC4, γC5) binding only to its cognate partner and showing no binding to alternate cPcdhs.
evaluation: Claims C42-C44 are supported by SPR data in Figure 2B and mutagenesis controls in Figure 2-figure supplement 1B. The extension of strict homophilic specificity to C-type cPcdhs strengthens the generality of the findings across the entire cPcdh family.

result: αC1 is an exception among C-type cPcdhs, not mediating cell-cell interactions in aggregation assays, and the recombinant EC1-4 fragment forms non-native disulfide-linked multimers, possibly due to incomplete calcium-coordinating residues in the EC3:EC4 linker.
evaluation: Claims C45-C47 are supported by prior literature (C45: Thu et al., 2014) and experimental observations from protein production (C46) combined with sequence analysis (C47). The inability to study αC1 is appropriately acknowledged as a limitation.

result: AUC measurements revealed a >200-fold range of trans homodimer binding affinities across cPcdh isoforms, from 2.9 μM (α7) to >500 μM (γC4).
evaluation: Claim C48 is supported by AUC data in Figure 2-source data 1. The wide range of affinities is notable and provides quantitative characterization of trans interactions, though all isoforms except αC1 mediate cell aggregation regardless of affinity (C49).

result: Despite varying trans-binding affinities, all cPcdhs except αC1 effectively mediate cell-cell interactions in cell aggregation assays.
evaluation: Claim C49 is supported by citations to prior literature (Schreiner and Weiner, 2010; Thu et al., 2014). This observation is important for interpreting the functional relevance of the measured affinity differences.

result: C-type cPcdhs αC2, γC3, and γC5 form trans dimers via EC1-4, but γC4 exhibits very weak trans dimerization (KD >500 μM) in solution, though full-length γC4 can mediate cell aggregation when delivered to the cell surface with a carrier cPcdh.
evaluation: Claims C50-C52 are supported by AUC data (Figure 2-source data 1) and prior literature (Thu et al., 2014). The weak trans affinity of γC4 motivates the structural studies that follow.

result: Two crystal structures of γC4 EC1-4 trans dimers were obtained at different pH values, revealing EC1-4-mediated head-to-tail dimers with different interface intactness (3800 Å² vs 2900 Å² buried surface area), possibly due to pH effects on histidine ionization or representing dynamic interaction states.
evaluation: Claims C53-C59 are supported by crystallographic data in Figure 3A-B and supplementary figures. The structural analysis is thorough, with appropriate comparison to other cPcdh structures (C59). The interpretation of pH effects (C57) and dynamic states (C58) is reasonable speculation supported by prior observations in related systems.

result: Structural analysis identified buried charges E78 and D290 in the γC4 trans interface as potentially destabilizing; mutagenesis showed that E78 mutations (E78A, E78Q) and S344R significantly increased binding affinity, while D290 mutations had no effect, indicating E78 plays an important role in weakening γC4's trans interaction.
evaluation: Claims C60-C64 are supported by structural analysis (Figure 3C) and AUC mutagenesis data (Figure 3D, Figure 3-figure supplement 1C). The experimental design is sound, testing specific hypotheses derived from structural observations. The conclusion that E78 weakens the interaction (C64) is well-supported, though the functional significance remains unclear as acknowledged.

result: SPR experiments with cis-interacting EC3-6 fragments revealed generally promiscuous cis binding (86% of pairs tested), but with a wide range of affinities (0.22-201 μM) and notably stronger heterophilic interactions between different subfamilies (particularly with γC3 and γC5) compared to homophilic and intrasubfamily interactions.
evaluation: Claims C65-C70 are supported by comprehensive SPR data in Figure 4A-B and AUC data in Figure 4-source data 1. The experimental design appropriately uses monomeric analytes for accurate KD determination (C65). The finding of preferential heterophilic cis interactions is a key result, though the functional implications remain uncertain.

result: The cis dimer interface is asymmetric, with one protomer engaging through EC5-6 and the other through EC6 only; alternate α-cPcdhs can only form the EC5-6 side and require a carrier cPcdh for cell surface delivery.
evaluation: Claims C71-C72 accurately summarize prior structural and functional work (Goodman et al., 2017; Thu et al., 2014). This provides essential context for interpreting the cis interaction preferences observed in the current study.

result: Structure-guided sequence analysis suggests γA-cPcdhs prefer the EC6-only side of the cis interface due to poorly conserved EC5 interfaces, while γC3 prefers the EC5-6 side based on residue differences that would disfavor EC6-only positioning; γA-cPcdhs form strong heterodimers with γC3 (low micromolar KDs).
evaluation: Claims C73-C75 combine inference from structural analysis (Figure 5A, Figure 5-figure supplement 1) with experimental SPR/AUC data (Figure 4). The reasoning is logical and supported by the weak homodimerization of both γA-cPcdhs and γC3, which is consistent with side preferences. However, the structural models used for hypothesis generation are acknowledged to be approximate.

result: SEC-MALS experiments with γA4/γC3 cis interface mutants demonstrate that the γA4/γC3 dimer has a preferred orientation with γA4 occupying the EC6-only position and γC3 the EC5-6 side, as mutations targeting the EC6-only interface in γA4 (V560R, K558R) abolished heterodimerization while the reverse mutations in γC3 had opposite effects.
evaluation: Claims C76-C79 are supported by SEC-MALS data in Figure 5B and SPR data in Figure 5-figure supplement 2B. The mutagenesis strategy is well-designed to test the structural hypothesis, and the results clearly support the proposed orientation preference. The asymmetric effects of mutations in γA4 vs γC3 provide strong evidence for oriented binding.

result: SPR experiments with γB7 cis interface mutants (Y532G targeting EC6-only, A570R targeting EC5-6) show that γA4/γB7 and γC3/γB7 heterodimers also have preferred orientations with γA4 and γC3 maintaining their EC6-only and EC5-6 preferences respectively; αC2 preferentially occupies the EC6-only side in αC2/γB7 dimers.
evaluation: Claims C80-C83 are supported by SPR data in Figure 5C. The mutagenesis approach extends the findings from γA4/γC3 to other heterodimer pairs. However, the interpretation for αC2 (C83) is noted to be based on limited data and would benefit from additional validation, as acknowledged in the text.

result: The strict homophilic specificity of cPcdh trans interactions is unusual compared to other cell-cell recognition protein families (type I/II cadherins, DIPs/Dprs, sidekicks, nectins, nonclustered δ-protocadherins), which show significant intrafamily heterophilic interactions.
evaluation: Claims C84-C86 are supported by the current SPR data (C84) and citations to prior literature on other adhesion families (C85-C86). The comparison appropriately contextualizes the exceptional specificity of cPcdhs within the broader landscape of cell recognition proteins.

result: High-fidelity homophilic interaction is a strict requirement of the chain-termination model and has been accomplished through a multidomain interface of ~4000 Å² that enables sufficient 'negative constraints' to preclude dimerization of ~1600 heterophilic pairs.
evaluation: Claim C87 is supported by citations to prior computational and structural work (Nicoludis et al., 2019; Sergeeva et al., 2020; Rubinstein et al., 2017). This provides theoretical context for understanding how the observed specificity is achieved structurally.

result: Systematic mutagenesis of five interfacial residues between β6 and β8 (which share 92% sequence identity) demonstrates that their highly specific homophilic properties can be attributed to these five residues, with the quintuple mutant exhibiting β8-like properties in both SPR and cell aggregation assays, while most single mutants retain β6-like properties.
evaluation: Claims C88-C91 are supported by SPR data (Figure 2-figure supplement 2B) and cell aggregation assays (Figure 2-figure supplement 2C). The systematic mutagenesis approach provides strong evidence that a small number of residues determine specificity despite high overall sequence identity. The consistency between SPR and cell aggregation results (C91) strengthens the conclusions.

result: Intrasubtype cis interactions are invariably weaker than intersubtype interactions, with β1, all γA-Pcdhs, and γC3 showing no measurable homodimeric cis interactions in solution AUC experiments; however, intrasubtype cis dimers likely assemble when constrained in native membrane environments due to 2D surface effects.
evaluation: Claims C92-C95 are supported by SPR data (Figure 4), AUC data (Figure 4-source data 1), and prior literature on membrane effects (Wu et al., 2013; Goodman et al., 2016a). The interpretation that weak solution interactions may be strengthened on membrane surfaces (C94-C95) is reasonable inference supported by prior observations, though direct experimental validation in membrane contexts would strengthen this conclusion.

result: While α cPcdhs and γC4 are obligate participants in cis heterodimers for cell surface transport, the remaining cPcdhs are preferentially, though not exclusively, participants in cis heterodimers.
evaluation: Claims C96-C97 are supported by integration of current SPR/AUC data with prior functional studies (Goodman et al., 2017; Thu et al., 2014). The distinction between obligate (α, γC4) and preferential (others) heterodimer formation is well-supported by the data.

result: Different cPcdh isoforms preferentially form one side of the asymmetric cis dimer interface, with homodimerization posing optimization challenges since the same residue must participate in different interactions on each side; however, carrier isoforms can likely fill both EC6 and EC5-6 roles as evidenced by robust cell surface delivery of single isoforms, suggesting side preferences are not absolute.
evaluation: Claims C98-C101 represent reasonable inferences from the experimental data on cis binding preferences combined with prior functional observations. The logic is sound, though the conclusions about flexibility in side preferences (C100-C101) are somewhat speculative and would benefit from more direct experimental validation.

result: cPcdhs from the three subfamilies have been shown to act cooperatively in certain neuronal contexts, though whether this relates to their cis interactions is unknown.
evaluation: Claim C102 is supported by citations to prior literature (Hasegawa et al., 2016; Ing-Esteves et al., 2018). This observation provides functional context for the cis interaction preferences observed, though the mechanistic connection remains to be established.

result: Possible functional advantages of weak homophilic cis interactions include ensuring diverse cis dimer formation at the cell surface and that homotypic zippers may be kinetically easier to form than heterotypic zippers.
evaluation: Claims C103-C104 represent speculative hypotheses about the functional implications of weak homophilic cis interactions. While the reasoning is logical, these are untested hypotheses that would require additional experimental work to validate. The authors appropriately present these as possibilities rather than established facts.

result: C-type cPcdhs have distinct expression patterns and functions compared to alternate cPcdhs: C-types are often highly expressed (e.g., in Purkinje cells), αC2 can mediate tiling alone, γC4 requires a carrier for cell surface expression and has unique roles in neuronal survival, and γC4 has much weaker trans affinity than other isoforms.
evaluation: Claims C105-C108 are supported by citations to prior literature on expression patterns (Esumi et al., 2005; Kaneko et al., 2006), tiling (Chen et al., 2017), neuronal survival (Garrett et al., 2019), and cell surface delivery (Thu et al., 2014), combined with the current AUC data on γC4 trans affinity. These observations provide important functional context for interpreting the binding data.

result: Different intracellular interactions likely account for specialized C-type cPcdh functions, with the cytoplasmic domain playing important roles in Wnt, WAVE, and other signaling cascades; for example, γC3 is the only isoform that can interact with and inhibit Axin1; extracellular interactions with other families like Neuroligins may also contribute to functional distinctions.
evaluation: Claims C109-C111 are supported by citations to prior literature on signaling (Chen et al., 2009; Fukuda et al., 2008; Keeler et al., 2015; Mah and Weiner, 2017; Onouchi et al., 2015; Pancho et al., 2020), Axin1 interaction (Mah et al., 2016), and Neuroligin interactions (Molumby et al., 2017; Steffen et al., 2021). These observations help explain functional diversity despite limited isoform number.

result: The study demonstrates remarkable tuning of cPcdh interactions: trans interactions are remarkably specific despite high sequence identity, while cis interactions are promiscuous but with binding preferences; these properties match requirements of the isoform-mismatch chain-termination model for neuronal self-recognition.
evaluation: Claims C112-C113 represent the main conclusions of the study, well-supported by the comprehensive SPR, AUC, crystallographic, and mutagenesis data presented throughout. The integration of trans specificity and cis promiscuity with the chain-termination model provides a coherent framework for understanding cPcdh-mediated neuronal identity.
